      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>? <p><span class="qt6">Head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span> is the name for <span class="qt2">cancers</span> that develop in the mouth, nose and sinuses, salivary glands, and throat and voice box (larynx). Most <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancers</span> are <span class="qt0">squamous</span> <span class="qt1">cell</span> <span class="qt2">cancers</span>. They begin in the moist tissues that line the <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span>. The <span class="qt2">cancer</span> <span class="qt1">cells</span> may spread into deeper tissue as the <span class="qt2">cancer</span> grows.</p><p>There are other <span class="qt2">cancers</span> that develop in the <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span>, such as brain <span class="qt2">cancer</span>, eye <span class="qt2">cancer</span>, and esophageal <span class="qt2">cancer</span>. But they are usually not considered to be <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancers</span>, because those types of <span class="qt2">cancer</span> and their treatments are different.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>? <p>Anyone can get <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span> is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over age 50.</li><li>Have a history of <span class="qt6">head</span> or <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>.</li><li>Have HPV (for <span class="qt2">cancers</span> in the tonsils and base of the tongue).</li><li>Are exposed to wood dusts or certain other toxic substances at work (for upper throat, nose, and sinus <span class="qt2">cancers</span>).</li><li>Have had radiation exposure to the <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> (for salivary gland <span class="qt2">cancer</span>).</li><li>Have Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection (for upper throat and salivary gland <span class="qt2">cancers</span>).</li><li>Are Asian (for upper throat <span class="qt2">cancer</span>).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>?<p>The symptoms of <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span> may include:</p><ul><li>A lump in the <span class="qt7">neck</span></li><li>A sore in the mouth or the throat that does not heal and may be painful</li><li>A sore throat that does not go away</li><li>Trouble swallowing</li><li>A change or hoarseness in the voice</li></ul><p>Other possible symptoms can depend on the specific type of <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>.</p>How is <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span> diagnosed?<p>Which exams and tests used to diagnose <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span> can depend on the specific type of <span class="qt2">cancer</span>. Possible exams and tests may include:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the area that might have <span class="qt2">cancer</span>.</li><li>Blood and/or urine tests.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect <span class="qt1">cells</span> from the area that might have <span class="qt2">cancer</span>. The <span class="qt1">cells</span> are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>?<p>The treatment for <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span> will depend on the specific type of <span class="qt2">cancer</span>, the stage (how advanced the <span class="qt2">cancer</span> is), your overall health, and other factors. The treatment options might include:</p><ul><li>Surgery</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li><span class="qt2">Cancer</span> immunotherapy</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that mainly attack specific <span class="qt2">cancer</span> <span class="qt1">cells</span> and cause less harm to normal <span class="qt1">cells</span></li></ul><p>In some cases, you may need a combination of treatments. Sometimes surgery can affect how well you can chew, swallow, or talk. Rehabilitation, such as physical therapy, dietary counseling, and speech therapy, may help.</p>Can <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span> be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li><li>Talking to your provider about HPV vaccination</li></ul><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2">Cancer</span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Skin <span class="qt2">Cancer</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>

      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Skin <span class="qt2">cancer</span> is the most common form of <span class="qt2">cancer</span> in the United States. The two most common types are basal <span class="qt1">cell</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span> and <span class="qt0">squamous</span> <span class="qt1">cell</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>. They usually form on the <span class="qt6">head</span>, face, <span class="qt7">neck</span>, hands, and arms. Another type of skin <span class="qt2">cancer, melanoma</span>, is more dangerous but less common. </p><p>Anyone can get skin <span class="qt2">cancer</span>, but it is more common in people who :</p><ul><li>	Spend a lot of time in the sun or have been sunburned</li><li>	Have light-colored skin, hair and eyes</li><li>	Have a family member with skin <span class="qt2">cancer</span></li><li>	Are over age 50</li></ul><p>You should have your doctor check any suspicious skin markings and any changes in the way your skin looks. Treatment is more likely to work well when <span class="qt2">cancer</span> is found early.  If not treated, some types of skin <span class="qt2">cancer</span> <span class="qt1">cells</span> can spread to other tissues and organs. Treatments include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, photodynamic therapy (PDT), and biologic therapy. PDT uses a drug and a type of laser light to kill <span class="qt2">cancer</span> <span class="qt1">cells</span>. Biologic therapy boosts your body's own ability to fight <span class="qt2">cancer</span>.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2">Cancer</span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Oral <span class="qt2">Cancer</span></content>

      <content name="FullSummary">What is oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span>? <p>Oral <span class="qt2">cancer is cancer</span> of the mouth. It is a type of <span class="qt6">head</span> and <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>. Most oral <span class="qt2">cancers</span> are <span class="qt0">squamous</span> <span class="qt1">cell</span> <span class="qt2">cancers</span>. They begin in the flat <span class="qt1">cells</span> that cover the surfaces of your mouth, tongue, and lips. The <span class="qt2">cancer</span> <span class="qt1">cells</span> may spread into deeper tissue as the <span class="qt2">cancer</span> grows.</p><p>Most oral <span class="qt2">cancers</span> are related to tobacco use, heavy alcohol use, or an HPV infection.</p>Who is more likely to develop oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span>?<p>Anyone can get oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span>, but you are more likely to develop it if you:</p><ul><li>Use tobacco or drink lots of alcohol. Your risk of developing oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span> is even higher if you do both.</li><li>Are male.</li><li>Are over ago 40.</li><li>Have HPV.</li><li>Have a history of <span class="qt6">head</span> or <span class="qt7">neck</span> <span class="qt2">cancer</span>.</li><li>Get frequent sun exposure (for lip <span class="qt2">cancer</span>).</li></ul>What are the symptoms of oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span>?<p>The symptoms of oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span> may include:</p><ul><li>A white or red patch in your mouth</li><li>A lip or mouth sore that won't heal</li><li>Bleeding, pain, or numbness in the lip or mouth</li><li>Loose teeth or dentures that no longer fit well</li><li>Problems or pain with swallowing</li><li>A lump in your <span class="qt7">neck</span></li><li>Ear pain</li><li>Trouble moving your mouth or jaw</li><li>Swelling of the jaw</li><li>A sore throat or feeling that something is caught in the throat</li></ul><p>If you have any of these symptoms for more than two weeks, see your health care provider or dentist. Oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span> can spread quickly, so it's important to find it early.</p>How is oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span> diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span>, your provider may use:</p><ul><li>A physical exam of the lips and mouth.</li><li>An endoscopy.</li><li>A biopsy or other procedure to collect <span class="qt1">cells</span> from the lip or oral cavity. The <span class="qt1">cells</span> are viewed under a microscope to find out if they are abnormal.</li><li>Imaging tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span>?<p>The treatments for oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span> include surgery, radiation therapy, or both. After surgery, some people also need chemotherapy to kill any <span class="qt2">cancer</span> <span class="qt1">cells</span> that are left.</p>Can oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span> be prevented?<p>There are steps you can take to help prevent oral <span class="qt2">cancer</span>:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol use or not drinking at all</li><li>Getting regular dental exams</li></ul><p>NIH: National <span class="qt2">Cancer</span> Institute</p></content>
